<!-- Every ### heading in this file is treated as a glossary term. Do not add other ### headings. -->

### Accelerator

Specialized hardware, such as a GPU or other device, designed to speed up particular computations.

### Access control

Policies, technologies, and procedures that determine who or what may access resources, under which conditions, and what actions are permitted. Requirements are usually established during project planning, based on data sensitivity and applicable agreements.

### AI problem formulation

The translation of a research question into a specific AI or machine learning task, such as classification, regression, segmentation, or generation. Formulation determines what data and labels are required and which models and evaluation metrics are appropriate.

### AI/ML workflow

An AI/ML (artificial intelligence or machine learning) workflow is the sequence of activities used to develop and apply an AI or machine learning system. These activities include data preparation, model development, training, evaluation, and reporting.

### Annotation

The process of adding labels, categories, metadata, or other descriptive information to data.

### Anonymization

Processing data so that individuals cannot reasonably be identified, subject to the limitations of the technique and available external information.

### Apache Spark

A distributed computing framework used to process large datasets across multiple machines or cores.

### ARX

A software tool for anonymizing and analyzing the privacy risks of structured datasets.

### Auditable infrastructure

Infrastructure designed so that its configuration, operations, access, and changes can be independently verified through records, logs, and documented controls. An auditor should be able to determine:

- Who performed an action?

- When was it performed?

- What was changed?

- Why was the change made?

- Was it authorized?

- Can the system's state be reconstructed?

### AutoML

Automated machine learning (AutoML) uses tools and services that automate parts of model development, such as hyperparameter search, architecture selection, or preprocessing choices. AutoML can reduce manual effort but may consume large amounts of computing time.

### Baseline model

A model used as a reference for comparing the performance of other models. Baseline models help researchers determine whether a new model or approach provides better results.

### Batch processing

Running computing tasks without continuous user interaction, often through a job scheduler. In HPC environments, training runs and other large workloads may be queued as individual jobs or job arrays.

### Batch size

The number of training examples a model processes before its parameters are updated. Larger batches require more memory on each GPU but can make fuller use of the available hardware.

### Bayesian optimization

A hyperparameter search that builds a probabilistic model of how settings affect performance and uses it to choose which combination to try next. The aim is to reach good settings with fewer training runs.

### Benchmark dataset

A dataset used to evaluate and compare AI models under consistent conditions. Benchmark datasets allow researchers to measure model performance using the same inputs and evaluation metrics.

### Benchmarking

The systematic evaluation and comparison of machine learning or AI models using specified datasets, tasks, metrics, and evaluation conditions. Benchmarking helps determine how models or model versions perform under comparable conditions.

### BERT

BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a transformer-based language model architecture that can be adapted for tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis.

### Bias

Systematic distortion or error in data, methods, or model results that can affect accuracy or produce unfair outcomes. Bias can arise during collection, preprocessing, training, evaluation, or use.

### Bokeh

A Python library for creating interactive, browser-based visualizations that allow researchers to explore datasets and examine patterns and relationships.

### Bottleneck

A component or step that limits the overall speed, scale, or performance of a workflow.

### Calibration plot

A plot used to assess how closely a model’s predicted probabilities correspond to observed outcomes. A well-calibrated model assigns probabilities that approximate how often the predicted event actually occurs.

### Categorical data

Data representing distinct categories, groups or labels, such as species, departments, or experimental conditions.

### Checkpointing

Periodically saving a model's current parameters and training state to storage. Checkpoints allow a training job to resume after a failure or a scheduler time limit, and they can require substantial storage capacity.

### Cloud egress

Data transferred out of a cloud provider’s infrastructure, often subject to usage charges.

### Community governance

A framework of rules, decision-making processes, roles, and shared norms that a group uses to manage itself and achieve common goals. Community governance emphasizes participation, transparency, shared responsibility, and stakeholder engagement in decision-making.

### Completeness

The extent to which required records, fields, or observations are present.

### Compute resource plan

An estimate of the computing capacity a project will require, covering CPU and GPU needs, memory, storage, data movement, job scheduling, and expected cost. The plan is also where choices among local, campus, cloud, and hybrid infrastructure are documented.

### Consistency

The extent to which data follows the same definitions, formats, units, and rules throughout a dataset.

### Container

A portable, packaged software environment containing code, dependencies, and configuration needed to run an application or workflow consistently across computing systems. Containers help make computational work reproducible.

### Containerization

Packaging software together with the dependencies it needs so that it runs consistently across computing systems. Planning for containers early makes it easier to move work between local, campus, and cloud resources.

### Controlled-access deposit

The submission of research data to a repository where access is restricted to approved users rather than made openly available. Access is governed by a review process and data-use conditions, which may reflect participant consent and institutional requirements.

### Convergence

The point at which further training produces little or no improvement in a model's loss or evaluation metrics. Slow or unstable convergence often signals a problem with the hyperparameters, the data, or the training setup.

### Correlation

A statistical relationship indicating how two variables tend to change in relation to one another. Correlation does not necessarily imply causation.

### Count matrix

A table showing raw integer counts of sequencing reads or molecules mapped to genomic features. The rows and columns represent entities such as genes and samples, and the cells contain observed counts.

### CPU

A central processing unit (CPU) is the general-purpose processor used to execute program instructions.

### CUI

Controlled unclassified information (CUI) is U.S. federal information that is not classified but requires safeguarding or controls on its handling or dissemination under applicable rules. Projects involving controlled unclassified information (CUI) may require approved computing environments and documented protective controls.

### Custodianship

The responsibility for the day-to-day management, protection, and operation of an asset on behalf of its owner. In data governance, information security, and research computing, a custodian is not usually the owner of the data or system. Instead, the custodian is responsible for implementing and maintaining the controls that protect it.

### Data acquisition

Obtaining data from sources such as instruments, databases, sensors, applications, archives, or external repositories.

### Data aggregation

Combining individual-level records into summaries or groups to reduce detail and, potentially, privacy risk.

### Data augmentation

Artificially expanding a training dataset by modifying or combining existing data, such as altering images, audio, or video, without collecting new real-world data.

### Data bias

A systematic distortion in data that can produce misleading analyses or unfair model behavior.

### Data cleaning

Identifying and correcting problems such as duplicates, missing values, outliers, formatting issues, and errors.

### Data distribution

The way values or observations are spread across a dataset.

### Data management plan

A data management plan (DMP) describes how data will be collected, stored, protected, shared, and retained over the life of a project and often beyond it. Funders frequently require a DMP, and it drives the storage, transfer, and backup resources a project will need.

### Data masking

Concealing sensitive values while preserving enough structure for a permitted use.

### Data pipeline

A sequence of automated or semi-automated steps that moves and transforms data from its source to its destination or analysis-ready form.

### Data preparation

The process of acquiring, cleaning, transforming, exploring, and curating raw data for analysis or machine learning.

### Data provenance

The documented history of data, including its origins, transformations, and movements throughout its lifecycle. Provenance records also capture who accessed or modified the data and how it was used. This metadata helps users assess the data’s history, authenticity, and trustworthiness.

### Data quality

The degree to which data is relevant, accurate, complete, consistent, reliable, valid, and usable for its intended purpose.

### Data transformation

Changing the structure, representation, scale, or content of data so that it can be analyzed or processed more effectively.

### Data type

The structural or semantic form of data, such as numerical, categorical, time-series, text, image, audio, video, or mixed data.

### Data validation

Checking whether data conforms to expected formats, ranges, rules, schemas, or scientific constraints.

### Data version control

The practice of tracking and managing changes to datasets over time so that specific versions can be identified, compared, and restored.

### Datasheet

Structured documentation describing a dataset’s origin, composition, collection methods, intended uses, limitations, and maintenance. Just as a model card documents an AI model, a datasheet documents the dataset used to train, validate, or test that model. “Datasheets for Datasets” is a well-known framework for producing this documentation.

### De-identification

Removing or modifying identifying information to reduce the possibility of linking data to an individual.

### Deployment

The process of making a trained AI model available for use in a research workflow or application. Deployment involves preparing the software and computing environment needed to run the model.

### Deployment plan

A description of how a completed model or workflow will be made available for use, including the environments, accounts, support channels, and ongoing costs involved. Planning deployment early distinguishes a one-time prototype from a service others will depend on.

### Differential privacy

A formal privacy approach that limits how much the presence or absence of an individual record can affect released results.

### diffprivlib

An open-source Python library developed by IBM Research that supports implementing differential privacy in data analysis and machine learning. It provides core privacy mechanisms, tools for statistical calculations, tracking privacy budgets, and drop-in differentially private equivalents for scikit-learn models.

### Dimensionality reduction

Reducing the number of features while attempting to retain important information.

### Disk I/O

Input and output operations involving storage devices. Heavy disk I/O can become a bottleneck when reading or writing large datasets.

### Distributed processing

Splitting a computation across multiple computers, processes, or nodes so that tasks can run concurrently.

### Distributed training

Running a single training job across multiple GPUs or compute nodes. Data parallelism gives each device a copy of the model and a different portion of the data, while model parallelism splits the model itself across devices.

### Dropout

A regularization technique that randomly ignores a portion of a model's units during each training step. The proportion ignored, known as the dropout rate, is set as a hyperparameter.

### DUA

A data use agreement (DUA) specifies how shared data may be accessed, used, stored, protected, and disclosed. A DUA may limit which collaborators and computing environments are permitted.

### Duplicate

Two or more records that represent the same observation or entity.

### DVC

Data Version Control (DVC) is an open-source software tool for tracking datasets, data transformations, and machine learning artifacts alongside code.

### Early stopping

Ending a training run once performance on the validation set stops improving. Early stopping limits overfitting and avoids spending computing time on training that no longer helps.

### Edge case

An unusual, extreme, or boundary situation that may expose weaknesses in a data-processing or analysis workflow.

### Encryption at rest

Protecting stored data through encryption.

### Encryption in transit

Protecting data while it moves between systems or locations.

### Encryption in use

Protecting data while it is being processed or actively used.

### Ensemble model

A model that combines the predictions of several models to produce a single result. Ensembles can improve accuracy and provide a measure of uncertainty, but they can also increase the computing and storage resources required.

### Epoch

One complete pass through the training dataset. The number of epochs is a hyperparameter and contributes directly to how long a training job runs.

### Experiment tracking

Recording the hyperparameters, code versions, metrics, and outputs associated with each training run. Experiment tracking makes it possible to compare runs and to identify which configuration produced a given result.

### Explainability

How well people can understand why an AI or machine learning model produced a particular result or decision.

### Exploratory data analysis

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) involves examining and visualizing data to understand distributions, patterns, relationships, anomalies, and potential problems before formal modeling.

### FAIR principles

Guiding principles for making research outputs, including data and related metadata, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. FAIR is widely referenced in funder requirements and informs planning decisions about documentation, identifiers, repositories, and curation.

### Fairness assessment

The evaluation of whether a machine learning or AI model’s outcomes meet fairness criteria appropriate to its intended context. This may involve comparing outcomes or error rates across groups using criteria that reflect relevant stakeholder, social, and technical considerations.

### Faker

A software library for generating realistic-looking but artificial data, often for testing or development.

### Feature

An input variable, attribute, or measurable property used by a machine learning model.

### Feature encoding

Converting data, often categorical data, into a numerical representation that a model can use.

### Feature engineering

Creating, selecting, encoding, transforming, or reducing input variables so they are more useful for machine learning and can be used in a model.

### Feature scaling

Adjusting numerical values to a common range or distribution, such as by standardization or min–max scaling.

### FERPA

The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) is a U.S. federal law protecting the privacy of student education records at covered educational institutions. FERPA gives parents and eligible students rights over education records and generally requires consent before personally identifiable information from those records is disclosed. Research using those records may be subject to FERPA requirements.

### Fine-tuning

Further training an existing pretrained AI model on additional data to adapt it to a particular task or research domain. Fine-tuning may update all model parameters or only a selected subset, typically requiring fewer resources than training a model from scratch.

### Formatting issue

An inconsistency in how data is represented, such as different date formats, inconsistent capitalization, or incompatible units.

### Foundation model

A large AI model trained on broad, general-purpose data that can be adapted to many different downstream tasks. Foundation models are usually reused and adapted rather than built from scratch, because training one requires very large datasets and substantial computing time.

### Generalization

How well a model performs on data it has not seen before. Improving generalization is the purpose of tuning decisions such as regularization, dropout, and early stopping.

### Git

A distributed version-control system commonly used to track changes to code, documentation, and configuration files.

### Go/No-Go decision point

A point scheduled in a project plan at which the team decides whether to continue, change direction, or stop, based on agreed evidence. Defining these points in advance limits the resources spent on approaches that are not working.

### GPU

A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a processor capable of performing many operations in parallel and is often used for machine learning workloads.

### Gradient accumulation

A training technique that combines information about how to adjust a model from several smaller batches before updating its parameters. This makes it possible to train with an effectively larger batch size than the available GPU memory would otherwise allow.

### Grid search

A hyperparameter search that evaluates every combination of a predefined set of values. Grid search is thorough but becomes computationally expensive as the number of hyperparameters grows.

### Hadoop

A collection of technologies for distributed storage and processing of large datasets.

### HIPAA

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) is a U.S. federal law that protects certain health information that can identify a person. Organizations subject to HIPAA must safeguard that information, which can restrict where and how it is stored, accessed, and processed.

### HPC

High-performance computing (HPC) refers to computing infrastructure designed to process large or complex workloads using powerful systems, parallelism, and specialized resources.

### HPO

Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is the process of systematically searching for hyperparameter values that produce the best model performance. HPO usually requires many training runs and is often submitted as a set of concurrent or queued jobs.

### Hybrid infrastructure

An arrangement in which a project uses a combination of local, campus, and cloud computing resources rather than a single environment. Hybrid approaches can address capacity or compliance limits but add complexity in data movement and cost tracking.

### Hyperparameter

A setting that controls how a model is trained but is not learned from the data, such as the learning rate, batch size, or number of epochs. Hyperparameter values are chosen before or between training runs and strongly affect the outcome.

### IDE

An integrated development environment (IDE) combines tools for writing, running, debugging, and managing code.

### Identifier

A field or value that identifies a person, organization, record, or other entity.

### Indexing

Creating an efficient lookup structure or identifier to improve data access, searches, or queries.

### Indigenous data governance

The principle and practice that Indigenous peoples hold authority over data about their communities, territories, and knowledge, including how it is collected, used, and shared. It is articulated through frameworks such as the CARE Principles and OCAP, and may apply even where no regulation requires it.

### Indigenous data sovereignty

The principle that Indigenous peoples and nations have authority over the collection, ownership, governance, use, and sharing of data about their communities, lands, and resources.

### Inference

The process of using a trained AI model to generate predictions or results from new data. Unlike training, inference uses what the model has already learned without updating its parameters.

### Interoperability

The ability of different systems, tools, or platforms to exchange and use data or functionality across environments. This capability often depends on shared standards, formats, or protocols.

### Interpretability

How well people can understand an AI or machine learning model's overall behavior and how it produces results.

### IRB

An institutional review board (IRB) is a committee that reviews and oversees research involving human subjects to confirm that it meets ethical and regulatory requirements. IRB review and the conditions it sets can determine where data may be stored and processed.

### Job scheduler

The software that queues submitted computing jobs and allocates shared cluster resources among users according to policy. Scheduler behavior, including queue limits and typical wait times, affects what project timelines are realistic.

### Jupyter notebook

An interactive document that combines executable code, outputs, visualizations, and explanatory text.

### Label Studio

A tool for creating and managing labeled datasets for machine-learning projects.

### Labeling scheme

A defined system for assigning labels or categories to observations, often for supervised machine learning.

### Learning rate

The hyperparameter that controls how much a model's parameters change in response to each update during training. A learning rate that is too high can keep the model from settling on a good solution, while one that is too low makes training unnecessarily slow.

### Lifecycle governance

The set of policies, processes, roles, and controls used to manage a system, dataset, or other asset from creation to retirement. The goal is to ensure that the asset remains secure, compliant, effective, and aligned with organizational objectives at every stage of its existence.

### LLM

A large language model (LLM) is trained on large collections of text to interpret and generate natural language. LLMs are applied to tasks such as summarization, classification, information extraction, and conversational applications.

### LoRA

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that inserts small trainable components into a model while leaving the original weights unchanged. LoRA reduces memory and computing requirements compared with full fine-tuning, potentially allowing researchers to use fewer GPUs.

### Loss function

A measure of how far a model's outputs are from the expected values, used to guide parameter updates during training. Loss values recorded across a training run are often plotted as a loss curve to show whether the model is improving.

### Maintainability

How readily a project's code, environments, and workflows can be understood, updated, and repaired by people other than their original authors. Maintainable projects depend on documentation, managed dependencies, and consistent computing environments.

### Matplotlib

A Python library for creating static and interactive visualizations to examine data distributions, patterns, and relationships.

### Metadata

Information that describes data, such as its origin, format, contents, collection conditions, ownership, or processing history.

### Missing value

A data field for which no value was recorded, collected, or retained.

### Mixed data

A dataset containing multiple data types, such as numerical, categorical, text, image, or time-series information.

### Mixed-precision training

Training that represents some values at lower numerical precision in order to reduce memory use and speed up computation. Mixed-precision training can allow larger models or batch sizes to fit on the same hardware.

### Model architecture

The structural design of a model, including the types of layers it uses and how they are connected. Architecture choices affect what kinds of data a model can handle, as well as the memory and computing resources it requires.

### Model card

A document describing a trained AI model’s intended uses, training and evaluation data, performance, capabilities, risks, and known limitations. It helps readers judge when and how the model is appropriate to use.

### Model evaluation

The process of assessing a model’s performance and behavior using data, metrics, and analyses suited to its intended use. Evaluation can include benchmarks and checks for bias or fairness when comparing models.

### Model license

The terms that govern how a model and its weights may be used, modified, and redistributed. License terms should be reviewed before a model is selected, because some restrict commercial use, redistribution, or use with particular types of data.

### Model parameters

The numerical values inside a model that are adjusted during training and that determine how the model produces its outputs. Parameter count is often used as a rough indicator of a model's size and of the resources needed to train or run it.

### Model performance

The degree to which a model performs as intended, assessed using metrics appropriate to the model type, intended use, and evaluation context.

### Model repository

A managed service for publishing, discovering, and downloading trained models together with their weights and documentation. Model repositories typically record version, license, and evaluation information for each model.

### Model serving

Making a trained AI model available to receive inputs and return predictions or results to users or applications. Model serving often uses an API to allow other software to interact with the model.

### Model weights

Numerical values learned during training that help determine how a model processes inputs and produces outputs. Weights may be saved and loaded for reuse or adaptation; pretrained weights may also be obtained from a model repository.

### Multicollinearity

A situation in which two or more features are strongly related to one another, potentially complicating model interpretation or estimation.

### Multimodal data

Data that combines multiple modalities, such as text, images, audio, video, sensor readings, or tabular measurements.

### Multimodal model

A model that accepts or produces more than one type of data, such as text together with images or audio. Multimodal models support research tasks that combine different kinds of evidence, such as pairing imaging data with written descriptions.

### NIST AI Risk Management Framework

A voluntary framework published by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology for identifying, assessing, and managing risks associated with AI systems. It is often used as a reference point when an institution has no AI policy of its own.

### NLP

Natural language processing (NLP) refers to methods for analyzing and processing human language in text or speech data.

### Normalization

Rescaling or restructuring data to make values more comparable or to meet the assumptions of a particular method.

### Numerical data

Data represented as numbers, such as measurements, counts, or continuous values.

### Object store

A storage system that manages data as objects, typically containing data, metadata, and a unique identifier rather than a traditional hierarchical file path.

### Objective & key results

A goal-setting method that pairs a stated objective with a small number of measurable results used to track progress toward it. OKRs are sometimes used to connect an AI project's technical milestones to broader research or institutional goals.

### Open-weight model

A model whose trained weights are published so that others can download, inspect, and adapt them. Open-weight models allow researchers to work on local or institutional infrastructure, although the accompanying license may still restrict certain uses.

### OpenDP

A software library available for R and Python that supports implementing differential privacy in statistical analyses. It provides tools for controlling how much information about individuals can be revealed in released results.

### OpenRefine

An interactive tool for cleaning, transforming, and reconciling messy tabular data.

### Outlier

An observation that differs substantially from the other observations in a dataset. Outliers may represent errors, rare events, or meaningful phenomena.

### Overfitting

When a model learns its training data too closely, including patterns that do not generalize to new data. Techniques such as regularization, dropout, and early stopping can help reduce overfitting.

### pandas

A Python library for manipulating and analyzing tabular and time-series data.

### Parallel processing

Executing multiple computational tasks at the same time, often using multiple CPU cores or GPUs.

### PEFT

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) refers to methods that adapt a pretrained model by training a small number of additional or selected parameters rather than all of them. PEFT substantially lowers the memory and computing resources needed to adapt large models.

### Performance profiling

The process of measuring how a program uses computing resources, such as CPUs, GPUs, memory, and storage. Performance profiling helps identify bottlenecks that slow down a model or computational workflow.

### PHI

Protected health information (PHI) is individually identifiable health information covered by HIPAA, including clinical, payment, and demographic data linked to a person's care. PHI generally must be handled only in environments approved for it.

### PI

A principal investigator (PI) is the researcher with primary responsibility for a project's scientific direction, funding, and compliance obligations. The PI is usually the person who must approve commitments of budget, data, and personnel.

### PII

Personally identifiable information (PII) is information that can identify a person directly or in combination with other data. PII may require additional controls on access, storage, sharing, and auditing.

### Pipeline monitoring

Observing a data pipeline’s performance, resource use, errors, data volumes, and processing delays.

### Plotly

A visualization library available for both R and Python that creates interactive charts. Researchers can explore data through features such as zooming, filtering, and hovering over individual observations.

### Population-based training

A tuning approach that trains several models at the same time and periodically copies and adjusts the settings of the better-performing ones. It combines hyperparameter search with ongoing training instead of treating them as separate steps.

### POSIX filesystem

A filesystem that follows common Unix/POSIX conventions for files, directories, permissions, and access.

### Pre-training

The initial training of a model on a large, general dataset before it is adapted to a specific task. Pre-training can require substantial computing resources, which is why researchers often reuse an existing pre-trained model instead.

### Precision–recall curve

A plot used to evaluate a classification model by showing the tradeoff between precision and recall. Precision measures how often positive predictions are correct, while recall measures how many of the actual positive cases the model successfully identifies.

### Problem statement

A concise description of the research problem an AI project is meant to address, including what is unknown and why it matters. The problem statement is what later decisions about data, methods, and computing resources are checked against.

### Project sustainability

The capacity of a project's data, code, models, and services to remain usable and supported after the initial funding or effort ends. Sustainability planning addresses who will maintain the work, on what infrastructure, and with what resources.

### PyDP

A Python library that supports implementing differential privacy in statistical calculations, including counts, sums, and averages. It is built on Google's differential privacy software.

### Quality assurance

Quality assurance (QA) involves activities used to check and improve data quality, including testing for completeness, consistency, bias, errors, and outliers.

### Quantization

Reducing the numerical precision used to represent and process a model’s values. Quantization can lower memory use and allow models to run on less powerful hardware, sometimes at the cost of accuracy.

### RACI chart

A planning table recording who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each task in a project. RACI charts help prevent gaps and duplicated effort in work that spans multiple teams or institutions.

### RAM

Random-access memory (RAM) holds data and programs while they are actively being processed.

### Random search

A hyperparameter search that samples combinations of values at random rather than testing all of them. Random search often identifies good settings using fewer training runs than grid search.

### Raw data

Data in its original or minimally processed form, before cleaning, transformation, labeling, or restructuring.

### RCD facilitator

A Research Computing and Data (RCD) facilitator works with researchers to turn research goals into workable technical plans and to connect them with appropriate resources, expertise, and institutional processes. Facilitators work at the interface between research needs and infrastructure rather than operating systems alone.

### Real-time inference

Using a trained AI model to produce results within an application's response-time requirements. Real-time inference is important for applications such as robotics, automated monitoring, and interactive AI systems.

### Regularization

Techniques that constrain a model during training to discourage it from fitting noise in the training data. Common approaches include penalties on parameter size, such as weight decay, along with dropout and early stopping.

### Repository

A managed system or service for storing, preserving, and providing access to research outputs such as data, code, images, publications, or models. Repositories may provide metadata, persistent identifiers, access controls, and other services that support discovery, reuse, and long-term preservation.

### Reproducibility

The ability to recreate computational research results by repeating a documented workflow with the same data or inputs. This depends on recording code, parameters, software environments, dependencies, and processing steps, and may yield the same or substantially similar results. Early planning for documentation, computing environments, and version control helps support reproducibility.

### Research Computing and Data

Research Computing and Data (RCD) encompasses the staff, infrastructure, and services that support computational and data-intensive research at an institution. RCD groups provide computing systems, storage, software support, training, and consultation.

### Robustness

The ability of an AI model to maintain reliable performance when given noisy, unexpected, or slightly altered inputs. Robust models are less likely to produce incorrect results when input data varies.

### Scalability

The ability of a computing system or workflow to handle growing workloads while maintaining acceptable performance. Scaling up a prototype may require additional CPUs, GPUs, memory, or computing nodes.

### scikit-learn

A Python library providing tools for data preprocessing, feature engineering, modeling, and evaluation.

### seaborn

A Python library built on Matplotlib that simplifies statistical visualizations, including comparisons between variables, distributions, and correlations.

### Secure enclave

A computing environment configured and documented specifically for restricted or sensitive data, with controlled access, monitoring, and limited data movement. Enclaves allow projects to work with regulated data on institutional infrastructure rather than general-purpose systems.

### Shared filesystem

A storage system that allows multiple users, computers, or compute nodes to access the same files.

### Slurm

A workload manager and job scheduler commonly used on HPC clusters to allocate resources and run batch jobs.

### smartnoise-synth

A Python library for generating synthetic tabular datasets using differential privacy. It allows researchers to create artificial data for analysis and sharing while limiting disclosure of information from the original dataset.

### Sociotechnical system

A system in which people, processes, organizations, and technology interact to produce outcomes. Understanding or improving such a system requires considering both its social and technical components.

### Software stack

The collection of programming languages, libraries, applications, operating-system components, and infrastructure used to perform a workflow.

### spaCy

A Python library for natural-language processing.

### Stakeholder mapping

Identifying people and groups with an interest in a project and clarifying their roles and needs. These may include researchers, intended users, collaborators, institutional offices, and support staff. Mapping stakeholders early helps identify requirements and approvals that might otherwise emerge later.

### Statistical summary

A compact description of a dataset using measures such as counts, averages, medians, ranges, variances, or distributions.

### Storage optimization

Organizing or transforming data to reduce storage use or improve read, write, and query performance.

### Success criteria

Conditions agreed upon in advance to determine whether a project has met its scientific, pedagogical, or operational goals. Defining the criteria for success early helps teams decide when a model meets project needs and further development is unnecessary.

### Support model

An agreed arrangement specifying who responds to problems, questions, and updates for a deployed model or workflow, and through which channels. Clearly defining support responsibilities and communication channels helps prevent expectations of indefinite support from individual staff.

### Synthetic data

Artificially generated data designed to resemble some properties of real data without directly reproducing the original records.

### Technical feasibility

An assessment of whether a proposed approach can actually be carried out with the available data, software, hardware, expertise, and time. Feasibility is often reviewed alongside policy and compliance questions before a project is approved.

### Test set

A separate portion of a dataset reserved for evaluating a model's final performance on data not used for training or tuning. Keeping the test set separate from the training and validation sets helps ensure an independent assessment of model performance.

### Text tokenization

Splitting text into smaller units—such as words, subwords, or characters—for processing by language models or other NLP systems.

### tidyverse

A collection of R packages designed for data import, cleaning, transformation, visualization, and analysis.

### Time-series data

Observations recorded in temporal order, often at regular intervals.

### Tracked transformation

A documented and versioned change applied to data, such as filtering, normalization, labeling, or feature creation.

### Training set

The portion of a dataset used to train a model by adjusting its parameters based on the examples provided. Keeping the training set separate from the validation and test sets helps prevent evaluation results from being influenced by data used to train the model.

### Transformer

A model architecture that uses attention mechanisms to weigh the relationships among elements of an input sequence. Most current language, vision, and multimodal foundation models are based on this architecture.

### Underfitting

When a model is too simple, or trained too briefly, to capture the patterns in its training data. An underfitted model performs poorly on both its training data and new data.

### Validation set

A separate portion of a dataset used during model development to evaluate performance and guide tuning decisions. Keeping the validation set separate from the training and test sets allows researchers to tune the model without using data reserved for final evaluation.

### Version control

A system for tracking changes to code, data, configuration, and other project files over time so that specific versions can be identified and restored. Version control supports documenting project history and connecting results to the materials used to produce them. Agreeing on version control practices at the outset avoids having to reconstruct project history later.
